summary: Rajesh finds Duolingo to be a fun and effective way to bond with his son over Japanese while feeling frustrated by some of the app's repetitive exercises.
top_quotes: You know, when I open Duolingo, I hope it makes me and my son feel like we're in a fun anime episode, learning without realizing!
The most helpful part is those quick lessons—like mini brain teasers that we can finish before breakfast.
Ah, but sometimes, the owl gets repetitive, I tell you, makes me feel like I'm stuck in a time loop or something!

interview_script.question: Intro greeting
interview_script.answer: Hello ji, how are you doing today? I'm Rajesh, nice to meet you!

interview_script.question: Short version of your life story?
interview_script.answer: Well, you see, I was born in Chennai, India, and moved to the US about 20 years ago. I've been in the IT field, you know, all that tech stuff, for quite some time now. Married with one son who loves anime. So, now I am trying to learn Japanese with him. It's a bonding experience, you see.

interview_script.question: Where did you grow up?
interview_script.answer: I grew up in Chennai, you know, the capital of Tamil Nadu, in India. It was a bustling city but still had its own charm, like a good masala dosa.

interview_script.question: What was it like growing up there?
interview_script.answer: Oh, it was quite lively, I must say. Lots of street cricket, festivals, and, of course, the delicious food. My fondest memories are of celebrating Pongal with the family, all those colors and sweets, you know.

interview_script.question: One turning point in your life?
interview_script.answer: Moving to the US was the big one, I think. It was quite a leap, like halwa falling into hot sambhar! But it was also quite exciting, new culture, new opportunities. I went to Houston first before settling here.

interview_script.question: Why was that a turning point?
interview_script.answer: Well, you see, it changed everything. Career-wise, it gave me opportunities that I didn't have back home. Personally, it was a big adjustment, adapting to a new culture and lifestyle. But, you know, it made me and my family stronger.

interview_script.question: How did you handle that situation?
interview_script.answer: Oh, a lot of learning on the job, so to speak. I just tried to keep an open mind, you know. Made some good friends along the way who helped me understand the nuances of living here.

interview_script.question: What do you care most about right now?
interview_script.answer: Right now, I think it's family time, yeah. I mean, work is always there, but these moments with my son, learning Japanese together, those are precious. It's like, who needs a TV when you have such live entertainment at home, right?

interview_script.question: Why is that important?
interview_script.answer: Because, you know, time is flying. One day he’ll be off to college, and I don’t want to miss these opportunities to bond and share experiences that we can laugh about in the future.

interview_script.question: What is a good day for you?
interview_script.answer: A good day? Oh, that's when I can finish work on time, maybe cook a nice Indian dinner, and then sit down with my son for some anime and a bit of Duolingo, just winding down without stress, you know.

interview_script.question: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
interview_script.answer: I think it's when I go to bed content. When I know the day had balance, a bit of work, a bit of family, a bit of learning, and, of course, some laughs.

interview_script.question: How do you make big decisions?
interview_script.answer: Ah, big decisions need a big cup of chai, you know. I usually mull over them, discuss with my wife, make a pros and cons list, and sometimes a little prayer for good measure.

interview_script.question: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
interview_script.answer: Oh, planner, definitely. I like to know what's coming, you know. Even in movies, I sometimes check online how it ends before watching!

interview_script.question: Example showing that?
interview_script.answer: Well, when we planned our last family vacation to California, I had an itinerary ready, down to the T. Even scheduled in 'flexible times' for surprises. My son teases me for that one.

interview_script.question: How do you handle risk?
interview_script.answer: Risk, I see it like spicy food. You enjoy it but handle it carefully. I try to evaluate, understand the worst-case scenario, and then decide how spicy I want it.

interview_script.question: Typical weekday?
interview_script.answer: Ah, let's see. I get up early, maybe around 6:30, start the day with a bit of yoga if I'm not too lazy. Then it's breakfast, helping my son with online school setup, then I dive into work. IT work can be quite demanding, so there's a lot of meetings. We try to have dinner together, and then some Japanese lessons or Duolingo sessions. We wind down watching an anime episode or two.

interview_script.question: Which parts take the most energy?
interview_script.answer: I think it's the juggling part, you know. Balancing work and family, especially with remote working, it gets tiring. Meetings, emails, and then shifting to family mode, it can be draining.

interview_script.question: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
interview_script.answer: More time for personal projects, I suppose. I've been wanting to, you know, dabble in some coding side projects or maybe learn to play the guitar. But the day just gets over too quickly.

interview_script.question: Biggest constraint last year?
interview_script.answer: I think time was the biggest constraint, especially with the pandemic. Working from home sounds nice, but it blurred the lines between work and personal life. Suddenly, work hours were all over the place.

interview_script.question: How do you deal with that constraint?
interview_script.answer: Ah, it's like managing a big traffic jam, you know. I started setting stricter boundaries, making sure I finished work by a certain time, and keeping weekends for family only. Even Sundays are no-screen time, at least till evening.

interview_script.question: People you feel closest to?
interview_script.answer: Definitely my family, my wife and son. And I've got a couple of close friends from college, we still chat and video call regularly. I guess it's the shared history that keeps us close.

interview_script.question: Describe those relationships.
interview_script.answer: Supportive, fun, and honest. We can talk about anything, you know. There's no judgment, just reliability. Like the old saying, 'a friend in need is a friend indeed.'

interview_script.question: Where do you spend most of your time?
interview_script.answer: These days, mostly at home, actually. Thanks to the remote work culture. In the living room or my little home office corner I set up.

interview_script.question: How do you feel in those spaces?
interview_script.answer: Oh, it's comfortable, but sometimes it feels a bit like the same scenery over and over again, you know. So, I try to add small changes, like new plants or rearranging furniture.

interview_script.question: What makes you feel that way?
interview_script.answer: I think it's the routine, the lack of travel and going outside lately. It's like eating your favorite dish every day—it gets monotonous.

interview_script.question: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
interview_script.answer: Mostly my wife. She's got a good head on her shoulders and usually has a different perspective. And if it's work-related, I'll talk to close colleagues or my old college friends.

interview_script.question: One tough moment in the last year?
interview_script.answer: Well, last year, my mother in India fell ill. Being so far away was tough, you know. I felt pretty helpless, and all I could do was make video calls and speak to doctors remotely with time zone differences.

interview_script.question: How did it affect you?
interview_script.answer: It was stressful, honestly. I felt this sense of guilt and worry continuously. It's not easy, juggling time between work, family here, and worrying about family back home.

interview_script.question: How did you cope?
interview_script.answer: I learned to prioritize and set small goals each day. Also, I leaned more on my friends and wife. They were my sounding board and helped me stay positive during a difficult time.

interview_script.question: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
interview_script.answer: Taking a break helps, going for a walk or doing some meditation. Sometimes, just watching a silly comedy with my son to laugh it off. Laughter really is the best medicine, I say.

interview_script.question: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
interview_script.answer: I would like a bit more balance, you know, between work and personal life. Maybe travel more with the family, see new places, and, of course, be somewhat fluent in Japanese by then. Wouldn't that be something?

interview_script.question: What do you want to be different?
interview_script.answer: I hope to be less caught up in work. It's important, yes, but family time should be higher on my priority list. Also, I want to dedicate time to hobbies, become more well-rounded, not just Rajesh-the-IT-guy.

interview_script.question: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
interview_script.answer: Oh, before Duolingo, we tried a book-based approach, you know, those 'Learn Japanese in 30 Days' kind of books. But they were more amusing paperweights than learning tools, I tell you. We also tried watching anime with subtitles to pick up phrases, but it was so random. Nothing seemed to stick!

interview_script.question: Most annoying part of old method?
interview_script.answer: It was not engaging, that's for sure. The books were very dry, and I would often find myself dozing off. Plus, the lack of interaction made it feel like a one-sided conversation, you know?

interview_script.question: Time it really failed?
interview_script.answer: One embarrassing moment was when I tried to use what I learned from the book at a Japanese restaurant. I ordered 'konnyaku' thinking it was some kind of special sushi but ended up with a jelly-like dish that my son teased me about for weeks!

interview_script.question: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: I first heard about it from a colleague at work. He was using it for Spanish and kept saying how fun it was. So, I thought, why not give it a try?

interview_script.question: What convinced you to try it?
interview_script.answer: The idea of learning while playing a game, honestly. My son and I are big on games, so anything that combines learning and fun is worth a shot. Plus, it's free, so there wasn't much to lose.

interview_script.question: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
interview_script.answer: So, let me think, just yesterday, my son and I sat down after dinner with the Duolingo app. We did a session on phrases, like 'konnichiwa' and 'arigatou'. The app gives you these little bursts of lessons, with matching words to pictures or repeating phrases. At the end, they have this funny sound for right answers and the owl mascot doing a dance. It’s quite amusing. My son loves it when we get a streak going, and he likes seeing our progress on the leaderboard.

interview_script.question: Most helpful part?
interview_script.answer: The quick lessons and immediate feedback, you know, especially when you match words with pictures or hear the correct pronunciation. It feels like solving a puzzle. Plus, doing it together with my son makes it competitive and fun.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part?
interview_script.answer: Ah, sometimes the repetition, I tell you. It’s like the app doesn’t believe I’ve learned 'konnichiwa' yet. It keeps throwing it at me like confetti. And if you make a mistake, no mercy, back to square one!

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
interview_script.answer: It must be the heart system, really. You make mistakes and lose lives, like in a video game. But here, it’s more annoying because sometimes the mistakes are typos or misclicks. Then you have to wait or pay to continue. Such a spoil sport, that owl!

interview_script.question: One time that frustration showed up?
interview_script.answer: Just last week, I was practicing 'shopping' vocabulary, and one little typo got all my hearts drained. I was like, come on, give me a break, don't be such a strict teacher! My son found it hilarious, but I had to take a break and recharge my hearts before continuing.

interview_script.question: Do you use workarounds?
interview_script.answer: Yes, yes, we do. Sometimes, if I know it's getting repetitive, we'll switch to watching an anime episode for some 'real-world' practice. Or use flashcards or other language apps for variety.

interview_script.question: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
interview_script.answer: They give variety, you know. Sometimes you need a change of scenery. The other apps or shows provide context and help connect words to situations better. Remembering vocabulary in real conversations, I think, is more effective that way.

interview_script.question: Worst-case scenario in this space?
interview_script.answer: I guess the worst thing would be, you know, if the fun and engagement are lost. Like if my son suddenly doesn't want to learn anymore because it feels like 'school' instead of fun time. That would be quite disappointing.

interview_script.question: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
interview_script.answer: I hope it makes learning feel like an adventure, like we are on some anime quest. And I hope we both can laugh and learn without feeling overwhelmed or bored. Something we look forward to every day.

interview_script.question: How do you know Duolingo worked?
interview_script.answer: Ah, when my son and I manage to throw a few Japanese phrases in our daily conversation, you know it's working. Or when we recognize words while watching anime and give each other high-fives, that's definitely a win!

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: I think maybe more focus on conversational practice, you know. Less 'fill in the blanks' and more dialogue simulations would be great. Make it feel like we're actually in a Japanese market asking for directions!

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
interview_script.answer: I'd love if language learning tools were more integrated, like connecting to cultural content—animes, food, music. Make it a full experience, like how we learned languages growing up, through life, not just books.

interview_script.question: Anything important we didn't cover?
interview_script.answer: I think we covered quite a bit, haha. Just that it's been a wonderful experience learning with my son, and I hope more people see language learning as a way to connect and enjoy, not just study.

interview_script.question: Permission to build a digital twin?
interview_script.answer: Oh, sure, as long as it doesn’t have to work overtime like me, ha! Go ahead, you have my permission.
